Grievous

/GREE-vus/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Grievous means very serious and severe, especially describing harm, injury, or damage.

Grievous means very serious and severe, especially describing harm, injury, or damage. One misplaced decimal in the bridge calculations was a grievous error, forcing engineers to tear out a year of work.

Worked Example

The night the freighter missed the channel, Keeper Anders rowed out through six-foot swells. He pulled three sailors from the water, but the second engineer had been thrown against the rocks. The doctor's telegram to the shipping company did not soften the news: the man's injuries were grievous, and he would never sail again.

Injuries severe enough to end a sailor's career — reported in the gravest possible terms — are what grievous conveys.

How Grievous Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

severe

Antonyms

minor

minor: small and not serious

slight

How Strong Is It? — serious → grievous → catastrophic

serious vs. grievous

serious vs. grievous: A serious injury demands attention, but a grievous one is graver still — severe and possibly permanent.

catastrophic vs. grievous

catastrophic vs. grievous: Catastrophic harm goes beyond even grievous — total disaster on the largest scale.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — griev-

Root — griev-: heavy, serious (Latin gravis, via Old French grever, 'to burden')

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of; having the quality of

Put it together

Put it together: Grievous descends from Latin gravis, 'heavy,' which passed through Old French grever, 'to burden,' before reaching English. The same heavy root underlies gravity, grave (serious), and grief itself. Gravel and groove only look related — their origins are entirely different.

Use the root in a new word: gravity

Use the root in a new word: gravity: Gravity — both the force that pulls us down and the seriousness of a situation — comes from Latin gravis, 'heavy,' the root that gives grievous its weight.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, somewhat literary

Grievous measures the severity of harm rather than naming a specific injury: a deep laceration (another word in this unit) might be grievous, but so can a betrayal or an error — no cut required. Grievous is also formal and a touch literary; in casual speech, 'serious' usually fits better.
